title: The sounds of Walden
hook: the train whistle, the owl, the bullfrogs: Walden's sounds (Walden 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bloom of the present: a doorway, sunrise to noon, and a broad margin to a life. Your line was the bloom of the present. Did a doorway get its ten minutes? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

A scream across the treetops, like a hawk over a farmyard. Then a rumble, and the cars of the railroad roll past the far edge of the pond. Later, church bells from distant towns, softened by miles of woods. At dusk, a whip-poor-will. At night, owls. And from the water's edge, a deep, absurd croaking that carries on into the night. It's easy to assume Thoreau went to the woods for silence. But the chapter right after Reading is called Sounds, and it's full of noise.
screen: `A SCREAM LIKE A HAWK.` → `BELLS, OWLS, FROGS.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: First, a second kind of reading. Sounds begins by turning from books. Thoreau warns that if we read only written languages, we may forget what he calls "the language which all things and events speak without metaphor." The world is also a text. Listening is how you read it. Second, the train. He doesn't pretend the railroad isn't there. The whistle cuts through his woods summer and winter. He's half annoyed and half thrilled. He watches the cars carry goods from far away, and notices townspeople setting their clocks by them. The modern world is part of the soundscape, and he listens to it too. Third, the bells and the birds. On some Sundays, he says, he could hear church bells from several towns. By the time the sound crossed the woods, it had changed, as if the pine needles on the horizon were the strings of a harp and the bell had swept across them. The distance made its own music. Then come the evening birds: the whip-poor-wills, and owls whose cries he describes as mournful and strange, and which he says he's glad are there. Fourth, the frogs. Late at night, the bullfrogs take over the pond, trumping to each other across the water. Thoreau writes their croak down as a long, rolling sound, and he clearly enjoys them. Nothing about this is holy in the usual sense. That's the point. Paying close attention turns a train, an owl and a frog into a kind of reading.
screen: `THE LANGUAGE OF ALL THINGS.` · `THE TRAIN IS PART OF IT.` · `BELLS THROUGH THE PINES.` · `FROGS ACROSS THE POND.` · then, large: `THE SOUNDS OF WALDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: five sounds. Settle and close your eyes, if that's comfortable. Breathe out. Now listen, the way Thoreau listened from his doorway. Find one sound. Name it to yourself, plainly: a fan, a car, a bird, your own breath. Then find a second. Keep going until you have five. Some will be near and some far. Some pleasant and some not. Don't sort them into good and bad. Just let each one be part of the place you're in. The bell holds the time.
The sounds of Walden. Thoreau's chapter of listening: the train whistle, distant bells, owls, bullfrogs, and what he calls the language all things and events speak without metaphor. Today's word.
Your line: sounds. Today, somewhere ordinary, a kitchen, a bus, a parking lot, stop and list five sounds you hear. Include the one you'd normally tune out. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden practice sitting still outdoors and naming what they hear, after the Sounds chapter, including the noises of roads and trains as well as birds.

fork.setup: you've moved to the woods for quiet, and a train whistle screams through the trees. what does Thoreau do with it?
options: complain and try to block it out.
listen to it too, as part of the place.
fork.reveal: he writes about the train at length, half annoyed and half thrilled, as one of the sounds of Walden.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sounds of Walden are peaceful nature sounds.
what it means: everything that reached his doorway, from bells and owls to frogs and the railroad.
what a scholar hears: a chapter placed right after Reading, offering listening as a second reading, of the language all things speak without metaphor.

notes: Verify the quoted phrase word for word against an 1854 text.

Paraphrases to check: the whistle of the locomotive penetrates his woods summer and winter, sounding like the scream of a hawk over a farmer's yard; people set their clocks by the cars; bells heard 'when the wind was favorable', the sound passing as if the pine needles in the horizon were the strings of a harp; whip-poor-wills chanting at evening; owls' mournful cries, and his gladness that there are owls; bullfrogs trumping at night.
